caption:
Why was Borobudur abandoned?

Nobody knows. The 9th-century temple in Central Java — nine stacked platforms, 2,672 relief panels, originally 504 Buddha statues — lay under volcanic ash and jungle growth for centuries. There are no records of its construction or its intended purpose either.

In 1814 Stamford Raffles, then British ruler of Java, was told about a big monument in the forest near Bumisegoro by local people. He sent the engineer Hermann Cornelius, who spent two months with 200 men cutting trees, burning vegetation and digging out earth. By 1835 the whole complex was uncovered. Raffles never visited the site, and is still credited with the rediscovery.

What came next was loss. Parts were taken as souvenirs, some with colonial-government consent. In 1896 King Chulalongkorn of Siam visited Java and was allowed to take home eight cartloads of sculpture. Of the 504 Buddhas, over 300 are damaged, mostly headless, and 43 are missing; heads sit in Amsterdam, Paris and London. Germany returned its collection in 2014 and paid to have the heads reattached.

Between 1975 and 1982 Indonesia and UNESCO dismantled over one million stones, catalogued them, and rebuilt the monument with proper drainage. It became a World Heritage Site in 1991.

Still open: when pilgrimage stopped, and why. A capital move after volcanic eruptions between 928 and 1006 is the most likely period. The original shape of the pinnacle is also unknown — Theodoor van Erp rebuilt it in 1911, then removed it, saying too few original stones survived.

Images: a panoramic view of Borobudur; a photograph from King Chulalongkorn's Java diary, 1896; O. Kurkdjian's gallery view, c. 1895–1915; a Borobudur Buddha head of 800–850 at the Rijksmuseum; Frank Hurley's 1913 terrace view; and Borobudur in 1973.
